performers: Kerstin Thorborg, contralto; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Carl Martin Öhmann sings the tenor songs of the same concert)
intro: “Der Einsame im Herbst”, marked “Etwas schleichend. Ermüdet”, is the second song of Das Lied von der Erde, sung here by Kerstin Thorborg. Muted violins play softly beneath a solo oboe, and the text tells of frost, a cold wind and a lamp gone out; the loudest passage sets a plea to the sun of love.

sections.label: A · Oboe solo over muted violins
sections.mNote: A solo oboe plays above quavers in the muted violins.

sections.label: B · Wind bending the flowers
sections.mNote: Clarinet trills accompany the alto’s line

sections.label: C · Strings without voice
sections.mNote: Violins and violas play a long crescendo

sections.label: A′ · Return of opening material, alto
sections.mNote: The moving quavers return beneath the alto line.

sections.label: D · Sun of love, E♭ major, alto
sections.mNote: Two harps play beneath the alto in E♭ major.

sections.label: Coda · Oboe and woodwinds after the voice
sections.mNote: The voice stops; the woodwinds play the closing bars.

cues.title: Solo oboe over muted violins
cues.text: Muted first violins play unbroken quavers. Above them a solo oboe, marked molto espressivo, begins a long melody. Mahler marks the movement Etwas schleichend. Ermüdet (somewhat creeping, weary), and the violin quavers continue while the oboe rests.
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score, p. 39: Etwas schleichend. Ermüdet, muted first violins and oboe marked molto espressivo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Source poem by Qian Qi
cues.text: The song is based on a poem by Qian Qi in which a woman weaves through a long autumn night beside a failing lamp. Judith Gautier’s French adaptation omitted the loom. The frost, the fading light and the loneliness passed through Hans Bethge’s German version to Mahler.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives prints Qian Qi’s Imitation of Old Poem: Long Autumn Night beside Gautier, Bethge and Mahler’s versions, identifying Gautier’s omissions. http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Einsame.htm

cues.title: First vocal stanza, alto
cues.text: The flute echoes the oboe. The alto enters in D minor with the first stanza, in which autumn mist drifts blue over a lake and frost lies on the grass like jade dust scattered by an artist. The moving violin line continues beneath the voice.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 39–41: flute Echo and opening vocal stanza. Mahler Archives supplies the German text and its earlier versions.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Bruno Walter, July 1908
cues.text: In July 1908, while he was composing these songs, Mahler was struggling with his doctors’ restrictions on exercise. He wrote to Bruno Walter: “I can’t work at a desk. For my inner activity I need outer activity.”
cues.evidence: Mahler to Bruno Walter, 18 July 1908, quoted by Stephen E. Hefling in his Universal Edition introduction, March 2010. https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Orchestral passage at figure 10
cues.text: After the lines about the golden lotus petals on the water, the singer stops. At figure 10 the violins and violas play a melody marked Zart drängend, zart leidenschaftlich, and the winds and horns crescendo with them. The cellos then play a diminuendo.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 43–44, figure 10: Zart drängend, zart leidenschaftlich in violins and violas, wind and horn crescendo, then cello diminuendo.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tempo I, figure 11
cues.text: The opening tempo returns at “Mein Herz ist müde” (my heart is weary). The alto sings p, without expression, over quavers in the violas and cellos. As the text tells of the little lamp going out with a crackle, the violas play am Steg, close to the bridge.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 44, figure 11: Tempo I, alto p ohne Ausdruck, viola and cello quavers, and am Steg in the violas under the lamp’s extinguishing.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Diagnosis of heart defect, 1907
cues.text: In July 1907, after Maria’s death, a doctor at Maiernigg found a valvular defect in Mahler’s heart, and a specialist in Vienna confirmed it. The defect was not fatal in itself, but such defects were known to lead to bacterial endocarditis, which killed him four years later. He set these words in July 1908.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s introduction for Universal Edition describes the diagnosis after Maria’s death, the specialist in Vienna and the link to bacterial endocarditis: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538 . The Mahler Foundation’s history page dates the composition of Lied 2 to July 1908: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-history/

cues.title: Figure 13, alto and solo violin
cues.text: At figure 13 the alto sings “Ich komm zu dir, traute Ruhestätte”, marked innig. A solo violin plays against the voice. Beneath them the strings continue in quavers.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 45, figure 13: Ich komm zu dir, traute Ruhestätte, alto innig, solo violin and continuing string quavers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harps in unison, E♭ major
cues.text: At figure 18, marked Mit großem Aufschwung, two harps play in unison under the voice in E♭ major as the singer asks whether the sun of love will never shine again. The voice holds “Liebe” across the bar, then moves on to the bitter tears.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 47–49, figure 18: Mit großem Aufschwung, E♭-major harmony, harps in unison and sustained Liebe.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Alto over pizzicato cellos
cues.text: The full orchestra drops out. Over pizzicato cellos, the alto asks whether the tears will ever be dried. Mahler added the word “mild” to Bethge’s poem, and the remaining music goes to the instruments.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 49, figure 19: Tempo I subito, p ohne Ausdruck and pizzicato cellos. Mahler Archives shows that mild is absent from Bethge’s text.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Munich, 1911
cues.text: Bruno Walter conducted the first performance in Munich on 20 November 1911, six months after Mahler’s death, with the Americans Sara Cahier and William Miller. At the alto’s entry in this song Mahler noted that, if necessary, the part may be sung by a baritone.
cues.evidence: The Berlin Philharmonic’s programme note by Tobias Bleek gives the première of 20 November 1911 in Munich under Walter, with Sarah Charles Cahier and William Miller, six months after Mahler’s death: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/gustav-mahler-das-lied-von-der-erde/ . The Universal Edition vocal score (U.E. 3391, French edition), p. 26, prints at the contralto’s entry “peut éventuellement être chanté par un Baryton”: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/b/bf/IMSLP177005-PMLP47886-lechantdelaterre00mahl.pdf

cues.title: Closing bars, violins and wind
cues.text: Oboe, bassoon and horn finish their phrases over continuing quavers in the first violins. The violins slow and hold their last note. A few wind notes remain, marked to die away.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 50: woodwind and horn phrases over first violins, final Rit., pianississimo violins and morendo wind chords.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Clarinet trills under the cold wind
transitions.from: A · Oboe solo over muted violins
transitions.how: The oboe’s phrase ends and the first violins, which have been moving, stop. Over soft winds the alto begins the second stanza, about flowers whose scent has gone. The voice is marked pp sehr gehalten. At the words ein kalter Wind the clarinets trill beneath the voice (full score, p. 42, figures 7–8).
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 42, figures 7–8: first-violin rests, pp sehr gehalten in the voice and clarinet trills beneath ein kalter Wind.

transitions.title: The solo cello joins the section
transitions.how: A solo cello follows the alto’s words about lotus petals on the water. At Zart drängend the singer stops and the full cello section joins the violins and violas. The strings play rising phrases, the woodwinds and horns enter, and all build towards a crescendo.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 43, figures 9–10: solo cello, Tutti and Zart drängend.

transitions.title: Cello diminuendo to pppp and Tempo I
transitions.to: A′ · Return of opening material, alto
transitions.how: The wind and string crescendo reaches fortissimo. The violins drop in volume, and the cellos repeat quavers in a diminuendo to pianississimo and then to pppp. At Tempo I the opening pace returns. The violas play the moving notes beneath the alto, who states plainly that the heart is weary.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 44: Wieder zurückhaltend, cello diminuendo to pppp, then figure 11, Tempo I.

transitions.title: Harps enter at figure 18
transitions.from: A′ · Return of opening material, alto
transitions.to: D · Sun of love, E♭ major, alto
transitions.how: The orchestra builds a crescendo after the alto’s long autumn phrases. At figure 18 (full score, pp. 47–48) two harps enter, playing arpeggios in unison. The music moves to E♭ major, marked Mit großem Aufschwung, and the alto begins a long phrase addressed to the sun of love. The winds drop to pianissimo under the start of this phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 47–48, figure 18: harps in unison, E♭ major, Mit großem Aufschwung and pianissimo winds.

transitions.title: Tempo I over plucked cellos
transitions.from: D · Sun of love, E♭ major, alto
transitions.to: Coda · Oboe and woodwinds after the voice
transitions.how: The harps keep playing as the alto presses on through the words about bitter tears, marked Drängend. Then Tempo I returns subito, and nearly every instrument stops. The singer finishes the question over plucked cellos. Bassoon and oboe begin the postlude (full score, pp. 49–50, figure 19).
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 49–50, figure 19: Drängend, Tempo I subito and the transition to the postlude.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, II. Der Einsame im Herbst, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 39–50: oboe and muted violins at the opening; string interlude at figure 10; Tempo I at figure 11; harp arpeggios at figures 17–19; woodwind postlude on p. 50.

timeline.note: Muted first violins begin; the solo oboe enters above their quavers.
Clarinets and horns join the oboe as both violin sections move in quavers.
Violas and cellos enter; the flute echoes the oboe.
The alto sings the first stanza over quiet winds and strings.
A long horn phrase accompanies the alto’s description of the frost.
Stopped horns, bassoons and bass clarinet sound a low chord beneath the voice.
The second stanza begins quietly over held woodwinds.
Clarinet trills accompany the alto’s words about the cold wind.
A solo cello answers the singer’s phrases about the golden leaves.
The singer rests while strings, woodwinds and horns make a long crescendo.
Fortissimo wind and string chords subside into the cellos’ repeated quavers.
Violas resume the moving quavers beneath the alto’s lines about her weary heart.
A solo violin answers the plea for rest, above muted horns and moving strings.
Flute and alto are heard above the first violins’ running semiquavers.
Two harps play in unison as the singer reaches towards the sun of love.
The first tempo returns; plucked cellos accompany the alto’s final question.
Bassoon, oboe and horn finish their phrases over the violin quavers.
The violin quavers slow to a held note beneath the last wind chords.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
